items.prompt: We’ve seen before how to say which fraction is greater. Here…  5/8  6/8
items.demo: …we can say that *six eighths* is greater, because it counts more eighths.  5/8 < 6/8

items.prompt: And here…  8/5  8/6
items.demo: …we can say that *eight fifths* is greater, because there are fewer parts per whole unit, and so each part is bigger.  8/5 > 8/6

items.prompt: But what do we do when the two fractions look like this?  3/4  7/10  The parts aren’t the same size. And they’re not counting the same number of parts.
items.demo: Well, to compare them, we rewrite them as *equivalent fractions*, and we make the bottom numbers the same each time.

items.prompt: First, we multiply by one each time:  3/4 × ▢/▢  7/10 × ▢/▢  Here, we multiply by ten over ten.
items.demo: 3/4 × *10/10*. Because ten was on the bottom of the second fraction.

items.prompt: And here, we multiply by four over four.  3/4 × 10/10  7/10 × ▢/▢
items.demo: 7/10 × *4/4*. Because four was on the bottom of the first fraction.

items.prompt: This will give us a pair of equivalent fractions.  3/4 × 10/10  7/10 × 4/4
items.demo: *30/40  28/40*. And each fraction has the same number on bottom.

items.prompt: If we want to compare these two fractions:  3/5  7/10  We multiply the first fraction by this…
And the second fraction by this…  3/5 × 10/10  7/10 × ▢/▢
Which gives us a pair of equivalent fractions.  3/5 × 10/10  7/10 × 5/5
items.demo: *30/50  35/50*. With the same number on the bottom.

items.prompt: Finally, if we want to compare these two fractions:  3/5  4/6  We multiply the first fraction by this…
And the second fraction by this…  3/5 × 6/6  4/6 × ▢/▢
Which gives us a pair of equivalent fractions.  3/5 × 6/6  4/6 × 5/5
items.demo: *18/30  20/30*. With the same number on the bottom.
